newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh ex-ruler Ershad's party faces split.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh ex-ruler Ershad's party faces split.

text.p: Two top dissidents in Bangladesh's Jatiya Party said on Friday they were trying to strip former president Hossain Mohammad Ershad of the party's chairmanship, virtually confirming the party's split.

"We have decided to call a national convention of the Jatiya Party later this month, where our effort will be to sack Ershad from the party's chairmanship," former deputy prime minister Shah Moazzem Hossain told reporters.
With him at a news conference on Friday was Kazi Zafar Ahmed, a senior Jatiya leader and former prime minister.
The duo have been at odds with Ershad over policy differences ever since he was freed on bail last January after six years in jail.
They have also criticised his much-publicised illicit love affair with fellow party legislator Zinat Hossain.
"He (Ershad) has blackened the party's image by womanising, especially his romance with Zinat that has even harmed his relationship with his wife Begum Roushan," Zafar told reporters.
"We can't support his filthy activities," he said.

A written statement, signed by Zafar and Moazzem and handed to reporters at the news conference, said the dissident leaders "wanted to free the Jatiya Party from Ershad's dictatorial leadership, turn it into a full-fledged opposition party and let it serve (the) people's cause".
They alleged Ershad had made Jatiya party an "extension of ruling Awami League and to serve interests of another country".
Although they did not name the country, it was obvious they were referring to arch-rival India. Opposition parties criticise the Awami League of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina as "India's lackey".
The dissidents paid tribute to Jatiya's secretary-general Anwar Hossain Manju for his effort to maintain the party's fragile unity, which they regretted would not be holding longer.
Ershad, smelling an almost certain rift, told a public rally in northern Bangladesh on Thursday that "Jatiya Party is a big tree and it can live without one or two branches".
The rift in the Jatiya, the country's third biggest party, surfaced in March when Ershad expelled Zafar from the party after he criticised the government's policies towards India.
However, he later withdrew the expulsion order under pressure from the party's rank and file.
Things appeared to unravel again soon when Ershad said in a newspaper interview that he had proposed to marry Zinat, wife of a former industry secretary, to "formalise" their 14-year relationship.
The former army strongman ruled Bangladesh for nearly nine years after seizing power in a 1982 bloodless coup, but was deposed in a people's uprising in December 1990 and sent to jail.
Ershad remained adamant over retaining his party leadership at all costs, his aides told reporters.
In April he dropped Zinat, a fellow legislator, from the Jatiya Party's presidium and stated publicly that his affair with her was over.
"But he still remains a tyrant in his dealings with the party and must be removed," Moazzem said.
